title: Active Directory SPN Flaws Let Attackers Steal Credentials Without Account Lockouts
content_md: Threat actors are increasingly exploiting overlooked Active Directory service principal name misconfigurations, making ordinary domain accounts vulnerable to Kerberoasting. The technique, called Ghost SPN by Trellix researchers , can allow an intruder to briefly assign an SPN, request a Kerberos ticket, and then revert the directory change before defenders fully identify it. Kerberoasting, tracked as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1558.003, enables an adversary holding a valid ticket-granting ticket to request ticket-granting service tickets for accounts associated with SPNs. Active Directory SPN Flaws Portions of those tickets are encrypted using keys derived from the target account password hash, creating material that attackers can crack offline at scale quietly. Unlike online password guessing, this process does not generate repeated failed logons or trigger account lockouts. An attacker can test captured ticket data outside the victim environment for as long as necessary. Weak, predictable, or reused passwords can therefore expose usable credentials, opening paths to lateral movement and privilege escalation. SPNs normally identify Kerberos-enabled services, including SQL Server databases, HTTP applications, and LDAP services. Because administrators associate them with service identities, audits often prioritize privileged accounts.
